verdict: WITHDRAWN — the ingestion oracle does not work at the density that matters, and addresses the wrong ingestion path

method.reference: Carlini et al., The Secret Sharer, USENIX Security 2019
method.model: character-level feedforward LM in numpy, gradients verified to 5.35e-08 relative error
method.canary: MATTER-REF-##### inside a fixed carrier sentence
method.rank: computed exactly via a digit-tree enumeration (11,111 forward rows, not 1.6M)
method.null: analytic — P(exposure >= x) = 2^-x by exchangeability, so p-values need no simulation

finding_1_null_distribution.observation: a canary that was never inserted scored 3.8 bits of exposure
finding_1_null_distribution.implication: an exposure figure alone is not evidence; p<0.001 requires ~10 bits

finding_2_ceiling_effect.observation: varying insertion count 1..64 at fixed corpus gave perfect exposure at every multiplicity
finding_2_ceiling_effect.implication: the model had memorised its whole corpus; the sweep was degenerate, not a result

finding_3_detection_floor.design: fixed compute (1.5M gradient examples), one occurrence, growing corpus

finding_4_capacity.implication: 4x the parameters buys ~3 bits; closing 7 orders of magnitude this way is not a plan

the_gap.assumption: a 5 KB document scraped once into a 10 TB (1e13 char) corpus

finding_5_wrong_threat.point: the oracle detects training-time ingestion; the threat this project addresses is inference-time (a document uploaded to a chatbot), which leaves no trace in weights at all
finding_5_wrong_threat.note: this required no experiment and should have been caught in design review

replacement: none needed — if a model's OUTPUT reproduces a per-recipient decoy, that is direct evidence of ingestion, identifies the copy, works at inference time, and needs no model access. Layer D already provides it.
biases_stated: small repetitive corpus and near-total memorisation (perplexity 1.08-1.18) favour the oracle
a fixed-context MLP memorises long canaries only through overlapping k-grams, which works against the oracle
params-per-example (~0.08-0.31) is broadly comparable to frontier params-per-token, but absolute scales differ by seven orders of magnitude and no extrapolation is claimed
